title: Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.
lead: Two nuclear licensing disputes reach the Court together, but the operating license, construction permit, and generic fuel-cycle rule retain separate records and questions.

actors.name: Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corporation
actors.role: Applicant for an operating license in Vernon, Vermont.

actors.name: Natural Resources Defense Council and other challengers
Atomic Energy Commission / Nuclear Regulatory Commission
actors.role: Regulator conducting licensing and generic rulemaking; functions transferred during the period.

actors.name: Consumers Power Company
actors.role: Applicant to construct two Midland, Michigan reactors in the companion case.

actors.name: Saginaw and Mapleton
actors.role: Intervening groups opposing the Midland project.

proceedings: The D.C. Circuit set aside the fuel-cycle rule and remanded Vermont Yankee’s licensing decision.
In the companion proceeding it required conservation analysis and elaboration of an advisory safety report.
The Supreme Court reversed both judgments and remanded, preserving ordinary substantive APA review.
limits: Seven Justices participated unanimously; Blackmun and Powell took no part. The Court did not finally validate the fuel-cycle rule’s substantive support or unconditionally approve the operating license.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Vermont Yankee’s license raises a fuel-cycle question
sections.cue: Why did the Commission move from one license to generic rulemaking?
paragraphs: Nuclear licensing separated construction permission from operating authority. Staff, the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards, and environmental reviewers examined applications; licensing boards held adjudicatory hearings with administrative review. Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corporation received a 1967 construction permit for its Vernon, Vermont plant and later sought an operating license. The licensing board excluded environmental effects of fuel reprocessing and radioactive-waste disposal, and the Appeal Board initially sustained that exclusion. Natural Resources Defense Council and other challengers contested the treatment.

The Atomic Energy Commission, whose licensing functions later transferred to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, then undertook generic rulemaking. It published alternatives based on an Environmental Survey and released the survey and underlying documents. Participants submitted written statements, made oral presentations as time permitted, appeared through counsel, and supplemented the record afterward. The Commission questioned speakers but provided neither discovery nor participant cross-examination.

Its 1974 rule assigned numerical fuel-cycle impact values for individual licensing cost-benefit analyses. It considered those effects relatively small and concluded that earlier licenses need not reopen on that account. The D.C. Circuit set the rule aside because opportunities to explore the technical evidence were inadequate, despite compliance with APA § 553 and additional opportunities. It consequently remanded the license. Interim rulemaking did not moot the dispute: the appellate judgment still exposed the license to reevaluation and possible revocation.

sources.pinpoint: Material Facts; Procedural History; 435 U.S. 525–530, 535–536 & n.14

sections.title: The Midland construction proceeding produces different objections
sections.cue: What did the intervenors and advisory committee actually contribute?
paragraphs: In a separate proceeding Consumers Power Company sought a permit for two reactors in Midland, Michigan. Its application underwent extensive safety and environmental review. An advisory committee report referred to generic safety issues addressed in other publicly available reports. Opposing groups included Saginaw and Mapleton. Saginaw filed many environmental contentions but declined meaningful participation in later evidentiary hearings and failed to identify supporting record findings. Its conservation suggestions did not become specific, adequately supported alternatives.

After the record closed, evolving guidance and another Commission decision addressed conservation more directly. The Commission declined to reopen and explained what showing would justify new inquiry. The D.C. Circuit nevertheless found the environmental statement deficient for omitting conservation alternatives and required fuller explanation of the advisory committee’s generic safety concerns. It also remanded fuel-cycle issues under its Vermont Yankee ruling. The Supreme Court reviewed the operating-license and construction-permit cases together; this did not merge their facts.

sources.pinpoint: Parties; Material Facts; Procedural History; 435 U.S. 530–537 & n.9

sections.title: Rehnquist identifies a judicial demand for extra procedure
sections.cue: Why could the court not prescribe what it thought would make a better hearing?
paragraphs: Justice Rehnquist wrote for all seven participating Justices. Although the D.C. Circuit disclaimed dictating an exact format, its criticism of opportunities to test evidence and its discussion of additional devices effectively conditioned validity on more procedure. Calling that meaningful participation did not supply authority to require it.

APA § 553 generally supplies what courts may demand for ordinary informal rulemaking: notice, opportunity to submit material, consideration of submissions, and reasons. Agencies may add useful procedures, but Congress had not given reviewing judges a general power to redesign rulemaking. Complexity and public importance alone did not justify discovery or cross-examination. Agencies possessed comparative ability to adapt process to their tasks.

A court judging the record afterward could otherwise impose requirements the agency could not anticipate. Defensive use of full trial safeguards in every rulemaking would erase Congress’s distinction between informal rules and adjudication. Written submissions, studies, and expertise can properly support a rule without a trial transcript, and cross-examination is not necessarily superior.

The Court preserved real legal qualifications. Individualized proceedings exceptionally affecting a small group might raise constitutional hearing duties, but NRDC did not maintain such a claim here. A wholly unjustified departure from longstanding agency procedure might also matter, but a few earlier proceedings using extra devices did not establish that practice. Constitutional requirements, statutory requirements, and exceptionally compelling circumstances remained distinct from judicial preference. NEPA required its actual environmental consideration and disclosure duties; it did not authorize general supplementation of APA procedure.

sources.pinpoint: Rule and Holding; Reasoning 1–6; 435 U.S. 523–525, 539–549 & nn.16–17, 21

sections.title: Substantive review survives the restriction on procedural invention
sections.cue: What could the D.C. Circuit still decide on remand?
paragraphs: Vermont Yankee argued that fuel reprocessing and waste effects need not be considered at all. The Commission by then accepted their relevance, and the Court held that their consideration lay within its authority. Waste followed from plant operation, and its persistence implicated the resource commitments NEPA addresses. That conclusion did not establish the accuracy of the numerical estimates.

A reviewing court could still find the rule’s contemporaneous explanation or record support insufficient under the APA. It ordinarily had to let the agency choose how to cure that deficiency. D.C. Circuit Judge Tamm had questioned substantive support, and the other panel members may have shared the concern. His concurrence was a lower-court opinion, not a separate Supreme Court writing. The remand expressly preserved arbitrary-and-capricious review; lack of support could still lead to vacatur and more agency consideration. The procedural holding did not make the rule or license unconditionally valid.

sections.title: The Court also rejects the Midland remands
sections.cue: Why were further conservation inquiry and report elaboration unwarranted on this record?
paragraphs: NEPA’s alternatives requirement was bounded by feasibility and what was reasonably known during the proceeding. Conservation guidance developed after the Midland statements and hearings. The Commission need not anticipate every future policy idea or reopen indefinitely. The record thoroughly examined conventional demand, and the intervenors did not develop a feasible contrary proposal.

The Commission retained an independent environmental duty, but could require timely, specific, material contentions sufficient to prompt reasonable inquiry. That was not a demand that intervenors prove a full civil-litigation prima facie case. Saginaw had opportunities to clarify and support its positions and did not use them; the threshold made the proceeding intelligible rather than abandoning NEPA.

The advisory committee primarily gave expert technical advice. Its references concerned generic issues documented publicly elsewhere. The D.C. Circuit required lay-readable elaboration and directed the licensing board to seek it without a request from any supposedly confused member of the public. The Supreme Court found no statutory basis for that extra step and considered it disproportionate in an otherwise extensive review.

The Court reversed both appellate judgments and remanded. Blackmun and Powell did not participate, and there were no separate Supreme Court opinions. The assigned excerpt focuses on fuel-cycle rulemaking; the full opinion supplies these companion issues and qualifications. Read beside State Farm, the distinction is between requiring reasoned consideration of an important alternative and choosing the evidentiary procedure used to produce it. Historical observations about technology and conservation are not present scientific conclusions.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning 9–11; Judgment; Separate Opinions; Notes; 435 U.S. 550–558
